title: Number our days
hookLine: teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom
carry: establish thou the work of our hands
last: NONE SPAKE A WORD UNTO HIM.

lines: TEACH US TO NUMBER OUR DAYS.
cards: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." That's a verse from Psalm 90, whose heading calls it a prayer of Moses, the man of God. It sounds almost like a math lesson.
Count your days. But the psalm around it is about how short a human life is, and it doesn't ask for more days. It asks to count the ones there are.
What does counting have to do with wisdom?

teach.b: First, God's clock. The psalm opens wide, with God before the mountains were born, and then says: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."
Time that feels endless to us passes, for God, like one short watch. Second, the grass.
People, the psalm says, are like grass: "In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth." One day, start to finish. Third, the count.

teach.h: SOON CUT OFF, AND WE FLY AWAY.
teach.b: The psalm puts numbers on it: seventy years, eighty if there's strength, "for it is soon cut off, and we fly away." Right after comes the verse: teach us to number our days. Not to dread them, and not to bargain for more.
To count them, so that we bring home a heart of wisdom. Counting is how you notice that something is limited, and noticing is how you start to treat it with care. Fourth, where it lands.
The psalm doesn't end on the grass.

teach.h: ESTABLISH THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.
teach.b: Its last words ask for something to last: "establish thou the work of our hands."
In some Jewish communities this psalm is part of the Sabbath and festival morning prayers, and it is sometimes read at funerals.
In a service of praise or beside a grave, the same verse sits in the middle of it, asking for a lesson in counting.

how: In some Jewish communities Psalm 90 is prayed in the morning prayers of the Sabbath and festivals, and it is sometimes read at funerals; Christians read it too, in their own services.

games.q: the psalm has just said life is soon cut off, and we fly away. what does it ask for next?
o: to be taught to number our days, for a heart of wisdom.
to be allowed to forget about death.
games.why: it asks to count, not to escape. and it closes by asking that the work of our hands be established.

practice: Count today, not the days left, just this one: on each breath out, count one thing it has already held, waking up, a cup of something warm, a voice, a stretch of quiet, a task done.

If you run out, count what's still ahead before you sleep. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line, so teach us to number our days; otherwise just keep counting, slowly, and notice how full the day is.
